headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Anaemia in Pregnancy
headings.content: Anaemia in pregnancy is a significant public health concern globally, particularly in developing nations like Nigeria where nutritional deficiencies and infectious diseases such as malaria are prevalent. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), anaemia in pregnancy is formally defined as a hemoglobin (Hb) concentration of less than 11 g/dL (or a hematocrit below 33%) at any time during gestation. During the first and third trimesters, a threshold of less than 11 g/dL applies, whereas in the second trimester, due to more pronounced physiological changes, a lower threshold of less than 10.5 g/dL is sometimes used. For nursing students, understanding these diagnostic criteria is critical for early identification during routine antenatal care (ANC) visits. Recognizing anaemia early prevents severe maternal and fetal complications, improving overall obstetric outcomes. Nurses play a frontline role in screening pregnant mothers, interpreting baseline laboratory investigations, and providing timely referrals or interventions. Untreated anaemia can swiftly transition from mild to severe, increasing the risk of obstetric emergencies such as postpartum hemorrhage and maternal mortality. Therefore, vigilance in assessing hemoglobin levels from the booking visit through delivery is a fundamental competency for every student midwife and nurse practicing in Nigeria.

headings.title: Physiological Haemodilution and Normal Haematological Changes
headings.content: During pregnancy, profound physiological adaptations occur to support the developing fetus and prepare the maternal body for labor. One of the most critical hematological changes is physiological haemodilution, often referred to as the anaemia of pregnancy. Throughout gestation, maternal blood volume increases by approximately 30 to 50 percent, peaking around the 32nd to 34th week. However, the plasma volume expands much more significantly (about 45 to 50 percent) compared to the increase in red blood cell mass (which increases by only 15 to 20 percent). This disparity creates a relative dilution of red blood cells, leading to lower measured hemoglobin and hematocrit values. It is vital for nursing students to distinguish this normal physiological adaptation from true pathological anaemia. Physiological haemodilution is a protective mechanism that reduces blood viscosity, enhances placental perfusion, and protects the mother against the blood loss typically associated with childbirth. Despite this expansion, a hemoglobin level dropping below 11 g/dL crosses the threshold into true pathological anaemia, requiring investigation and treatment. Recognizing the boundaries between normal haemodilution and pathological states ensures that nurses do not unnecessarily alarm mothers while remaining alert to genuine nutritional or pathological deficits.

headings.title: Classification and Etiology of Anaemia in Pregnancy
headings.content: Anaemia in pregnancy can be classified based on its etiology and red blood cell morphology. The most common type is iron-deficiency anaemia (IDA), accounting for up to 75-80% of cases in developing countries, driven by inadequate dietary intake, depleted iron stores, and increased fetal demand. Megaloblastic anaemia, caused by folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, is another nutritional type characterized by large, immature red blood cells. In regions like Nigeria, haemolytic anemias such as sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbSC) and malaria-induced hemolysis are major contributors to maternal morbidity. Acute blood loss, hookworm infestations, and chronic inflammatory conditions also precipitate or worsen anaemia. Nurses must understand these underlying etiologies because treatment differs vastly depending on the root cause. For instance, while iron-deficiency anaemia responds to iron supplementation, megaloblastic anaemia requires folic acid, and sickle cell crises require comprehensive multidisciplinary management including hydration, pain relief, and possibly blood transfusions. Identifying the specific etiology during antenatal booking enables targeted, effective clinical management that safeguards both mother and child throughout the gestational journey.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment in Pregnant Women
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of anaemia in pregnancy can often be insidious, developing gradually as hemoglobin levels decline. Mild anaemia may be entirely asymptomatic, discovered only during routine antenatal blood screening. As anaemia worsens, symptoms become more apparent due to tissue hypoxia. Common complaints include generalized fatigue, generalized weakness, pallor of the skin, conjunctivae, nail beds, and palmar creases. Patients frequently report exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, dizziness, and headaches. In severe cases, signs of high-output cardiac failure can manifest, including tachycardia, peripheral edema, and basal crackles in the lungs. During the physical assessment, nurses must systematically inspect mucosal barriers and palpate for organomegaly, such as splenomegaly associated with haemolytic conditions. A thorough history should explore dietary habits, pica (the compulsive eating of non-food items like clay or ice), previous obstetric history, and symptoms of concurrent infections like malaria or hookworm. Recognizing these clinical signs promptly allows nursing students to advocate for immediate medical evaluation and laboratory confirmation, preventing escalation into life-threatening maternal emergencies.

headings.title: Diagnostic Investigations and Laboratory Findings
headings.content: Accurate diagnosis of anaemia and its underlying causes relies on systematic laboratory investigations initiated at the first antenatal visit and repeated at strategic gestational intervals. The cornerstone test is the hemoglobin (Hb) concentration or packed cell volume (PCV) estimation. Further investigations include red blood cell indices such as mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), and peripheral blood film microscopy, which helps identify microcytic, macrocytic, or normocytic morphologies. Serum ferritin is the gold standard test for assessing iron stores, while serum iron and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) provide additional clarity. In malaria-endemic regions like Nigeria, screening tests such as malaria parasite microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are mandatory. Genotyping (hemoglobin electrophoresis) must be performed to rule out hemoglobinopathies like sickle cell trait or disease. Urinalysis and stool microscopy are also useful to detect urinary tract infections or gastrointestinal parasite infestations like hookworms. Student nurses must understand these laboratory parameters to effectively collaborate with the multidisciplinary healthcare team in formulating accurate diagnoses and tailored treatment regimens.

headings.title: Maternal and Fetal Complications of Anaemia
headings.content: Anaemia poses severe risks to both the mother and the developing fetus, making its prevention and management a top priority in obstetric care. Maternal complications include increased susceptibility to infections, postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) due to poor uterine muscle tone and reduced blood tolerance, delayed wound healing following episiotomy or cesarean section, and an elevated risk of maternal mortality. In severe cases, anaemia can precipitate congestive heart failure and cardiogenic shock. Fetal and neonatal complications are equally alarming; they include intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), low birth weight (LBW), preterm birth, fetal distress, and increased perinatal and neonatal mortality. Furthermore, infants born to severely anaemic mothers often have depleted iron stores, predisposing them to early infancy anaemia and impaired cognitive and motor development. Student nurses must comprehend these cascading risks to communicate the urgency of treatment compliance to pregnant women and their families, reinforcing that managing anaemia is vital for safeguarding two lives simultaneously.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of anaemia in pregnancy focuses on correcting hemoglobin deficits, replenishing nutrient stores, and treating underlying causes. For iron-deficiency anaemia, oral iron supplements (such as ferrous sulfate, ferrous fumarate, or ferrous gluconate) combined with folic acid are routinely prescribed as prophylaxis and treatment. Nurses must educate patients on taking iron supplements with vitamin C (like citrus juices) to enhance absorption while avoiding tea, coffee, or milk which inhibit absorption. Gastrointestinal side effects like constipation, nausea, and dark stools are common and often lead to poor compliance; nurses must counsel patients on managing these effects without stopping medication. In cases of severe anaemia, severe third-trimester presentation, intolerance to oral iron, or malabsorption, parenteral iron therapy (such as iron sucrose or iron dextran) or blood transfusions may be indicated. Additionally, management must include intermittent preventive treatment for malaria (IPTp) using sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and routine deworming where applicable, ensuring a comprehensive pharmacological approach to maternal wellness.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Health Education in Antenatal Care
headings.content: Nursing care and health education form the bedrock of successful antenatal management of anaemia. The nursing care plan involves continuous assessment of vital signs, monitoring PCV/Hb levels, evaluating dietary intake, and observing for signs of complications or medication side effects. Health education should be delivered in culturally sensitive, clear language, emphasizing the importance of a balanced, iron-rich diet containing green leafy vegetables, beans, lean meats, and local sources of protein and vitamins. Nurses must instruct mothers on proper adherence to prescribed routine hematinics and explain how to manage minor side effects like dark stools or mild constipation. Furthermore, nurses should educate patients on malaria prevention strategies, including the consistent use of insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) and taking prescribed IPTp doses. Empowering pregnant women with knowledge encourages active participation in their healthcare, improves treatment compliance, reduces hospital readmissions, and ultimately promotes safe motherhood and healthy neonatal outcomes across Nigerian communities.
